hook: A Victorian chess-playing machine with a very dark secret at its center, told through procedures, an intake report and staff emails. The page uses visual tricks near the end, so read it somewhere they can play out. Be ready for human remains of children and a symptom list that ends in self-harm.
whyItMatters: It sets the touring chess automaton, the sort of sideshow curiosity its intake report compares to the Turk, against an infohazard that spreads through networked computers. That mix of nineteenth-century showmanship and modern email horror gives it a distinct texture. It also leans on format, letting garbled symbols and a stuck upload bar do work that prose could not.
thingsToNotice:
The opening note already tells you this ends badly: an exercise marked both in progress and cancelled, plus a new ban on wireless networks. The description then states the secret flatly: the machine's analytical engine is built from the combined brain tissue of a Russian chess prodigy's twin daughters, and the bone pieces carved in the Oriental style match their DNA.

The intake report still files the newspaper story about the champion's missing fourteen-year-old twins as unconnected, and the staff roster quietly includes a child psychologist. Watch the speed lever too: each setting is a clean, measurable step until setting V, where play slides from brilliant to illegal moves to pieces being rammed together hard enough to chip. Minutes later an email arrives with a stretched photo of two girls and a Russian-named executable, and its symptom timeline runs from anxiety to children's laughter, a brief false recovery in which victims demand the infected computer, self-mutilation at twelve hours and a redaction at fourteen. The final addenda give up on readable text altogether, ending on an upload that never finishes, which suits a file that is itself being taken over.
